Besides submitting a proposal on the commission structure for in-app purchases (IAP) completed through non-App Store systems within the United States, Apple has also filed a motion expressing willingness to explore the possibility of reaching a settlement with Epic Games. Details are as follows.

Apple may be ready to settle

Apple earlier submitted a proposal outlining its hope to be allowed to charge commissions on transactions completed through payment systems outside the App Store.

The timing of Apple's filing coincides with the Supreme Court denying Apple's application to stay lower court proceedings during its review of Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers's civil contempt ruling against Apple. That ruling found Apple in contempt for continuing to charge a 27% commission after the court had ordered it to allow developers to direct users to external payment methods.

Under Apple's proposed framework, Apple could charge up to a 15% commission on transactions completed through alternative payment systems. Epic Games immediately objected, stating that it "believes these fees far exceed the permissible fee guidelines set by the Ninth Circuit."

Although that document attracted considerable attention, Apple today also separately filed a motion requesting Judge Gonzalez Rogers to order both parties to attend a settlement conference.

Document excerpt (edited for clarity):

In other words, Apple's legal team had actually contacted Epic's lawyers before filing the motion to discuss applying for a settlement conference, but Epic did not agree to this request.

Apple stated in the filing that the court has the authority to order both parties to attend a settlement conference without Epic's consent, adding that the Ninth Circuit itself also encouraged both parties to reach an agreement on appropriate external link commissions.

Apple also noted that "discussing potential settlement options in a confidential, non-adversarial environment would increase the likelihood of reaching a pragmatic solution, thereby avoiding lengthy remand proceedings."

It is worth noting that this filing does not contain any settlement proposal or offer from Apple, nor does it constitute an actual settlement suggestion. Apple is effectively requesting the court to order both parties to conduct settlement negotiations under the supervision of Magistrate Judge Joseph C. Spero.
